analysis.one_liner: Requires employers with 15 or more workers to let employees earn up to seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: The bill had 136 House supporters — all Democrats — but was sent to three committees and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Healthy Families Act would require employers with 15 or more employees to let workers earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours (seven days) a year [S2][S3]. Workers could use the time for their own illness, a doctor's visit, caring for a sick child or family member, or dealing with domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking [S2][S3]. Employers with existing paid-leave policies that already meet the standard would not have to add anything [S3]. The bill never advanced past its committee referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers without paid sick leave and their families. The bill's own findings state that nearly 40 percent of the private-sector workforce lacks paid sick time, including 71 percent of the lowest-paid quartile of workers, and millions more cannot use existing leave to care for a sick child or family member [S3]. Workers dealing with domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking would get protected time for medical care, relocation, or court proceedings [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers without paid sick leave

how_it_helps.text: Lets employees at covered employers earn 1 hour of paid sick time per 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year, usable for their own medical needs and those of family members

Covers domestic violence, sexual assault, and stalking: paid time to seek medical attention, get counseling, relocate, or take legal action, with flexible documentation rules and confidentiality protections
Bars employers from firing, retaliating against, or counting sick days against workers under attendance policies, and lets workers sue or complain to the Labor Department when violated

The bill's findings cite studies linking paid sick leave to higher preventive care use, fewer children sent to school sick, and an estimated $1.1 billion per year in reduced emergency-room costs, including $500 million in Medicaid savings

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees, who would pay for up to 56 hours of sick time per worker per year (or confirm existing leave meets the standard) and handle record-keeping and certification. Workers would not pay directly, though employers might absorb the cost through wages or prices.

drawbacks.text: The mandate falls on employers: businesses with 15 or more employees would fund up to seven sick days per worker per year and manage certification, record-keeping, and notice requirements

Employers may require a health care provider's certification for absences longer than three consecutive workdays, which imposes a documentation burden on workers who must see a doctor to justify short absences
The 15-employee threshold leaves workers at smaller businesses — often those least likely to have paid sick leave — with no new protection under this bill

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 40 percent of private-sector workers lacking paid sick time — concentrated among the lowest-paid — the bill offers a concrete benefit, and the bill's findings argue that early care and reduced presenteeism offset part of the employer cost. The genuine trade-off is a new paid-benefit mandate on employers, and the bill's design choices (a 15-employee floor, a 56-hour annual cap, credit for existing policies, no payout of unused time at separation) were written to limit that cost.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: after being referred to three committees and then two subcommittees, no hearing or vote ever happened, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Healthy Families Act on March 20, 2013, with 92 original cosponsors
The bill was referred to the Education and the Workforce, House Administration, and Oversight and Government Reform Committees
On April 23, 2013, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions and the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections — its last recorded action
No further action was taken, and the bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have borne the cost of the paid sick day mandate are better off, since the bill never advanced. Workers without paid sick leave — the bill's findings say nearly 40 percent of the private-sector workforce — gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have paid for sick leave

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized an initial list of 92 cosponsors

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction, referred it to two subcommittees, and never scheduled a hearing or markup; no further action appears in the record

against.name: Speaker of the House
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with Republican control of the chamber, a bill reported out of committee would still have needed the Speaker to schedule a vote

sides.party_line_note: All 135 cosponsors were House Democrats, with no Republican support listed; the House was under Republican control, and the bill never advanced past subcommittee referral.

industries.industry: Employers with 15 or more employees (especially retail, food service, and other low-wage service sectors)
industries.note: These employers would pay for up to 56 hours of sick time per worker per year and handle compliance costs. The bill's findings argue part of the cost is offset by reduced turnover and presenteeism, but the mandate is a direct new expense, and it is the reason such bills typically face unified business opposition.

industries.industry: Small businesses with fewer than 15 employees
industries.note: They are exempt from the mandate, so they face no compliance cost under this bill, though their workers also get no new benefit.
